title: Minimalist training bad
summary: An hour-long essay on minimalism in training: a useful corrective against maximalist programs that swung too far, spread by strength sports where specificity rules but harmful to bodybuilders. He lists minimalist traits, defends isolation and adding volume over time, and contrasts reductionism with perfectionism.
claims: Junk volume is not bad in itself; it is only bad when it replaces meaningful volume
Training minimalism appeared about 10 years ago in response to overloaded programs, cut the fluff, and rightly recentered fitness on the basics
Doing more does not mean progressing more; most lifters are maximalists by default and need a dose of minimalism
Once maximalism was defeated, minimalism kept swinging like a pendulum and turned on itself until it became harmful to gains
Strength sports (powerlifting, calisthenics, Olympic weightlifting) are minimalist by default, while bodybuilding is maximalist by default
The more specific the needs, the more minimalist the method; strength athletes should be minimalist
Strength athletes train functions; bodybuilders train muscles. A powerlifter squats to train his squat, a bodybuilder to train quads, glutes, hamstrings and hips
A powerlifter training only for bigger quads will not raise his squat much, and a bodybuilder training only for a stronger squat will not grow his legs much
Even top powerlifters and weightlifters use variations like pause squats that feed the main lift, so pure minimalism fails even for strength
Specificity still matters for bodybuilders: keep lifts in a line of specificity so they keep progressing
You can spot a minimalist by phrases like 'just do X instead': they keep shrinking programs even when nothing needs fixing
Minimalists cut exercise selection and workout length the way cost-cutting consultants slash budgets, chasing performance
Shunning isolation is a minimalist trait inherited from strength athletes; curls after squats do not hurt squat recovery, so do both
Correct skull crusher: go to maximum shoulder flexion, lock the shoulder and move only the elbow to stretch the long head; the swinging version is a pullover driven by the lats
Lifting the elbows on curls brings in the shoulders and more weight but not more biceps work; keep elbows at your sides
HIT is minimalism born in bodybuilding; one set cannot make up for lost sets because reps and sets compound, and the claim that extra sets are wasted is false
Training a body part once a week for the rest of your life makes no sense
Prioritizing instantaneous strength over long-term progression kills bodybuilding; avoiding supersets to save 2% performance is irrational when the extra exercise adds ten times the tonnage
Strength work opens the workout as preparation, but most hypertrophic tonnage comes from what follows; slashing the rest makes you a strength athlete who stops growing
One-lift-a-day and Bulgarian methods drive strength on the lift but build little muscle; their big proponents do lots of side volume after decades of training
Use minimalism as a tool, not an ideology; he trims about 20% from famous programs because five exercises of four sets for one muscle is overkill
Do just the sets needed to damage the fibers, recover and progress, no more and no less
Minimalism works for leg day: squats and deadlifts make beginners grow; reduce frequency and add variations over time
Novices get to be minimalist, but Starting Strength is minimalist to a fault: novices need to train every muscle group with isolation work too
Many minimalist gurus only speak to novices and are out of their depth with intermediate and advanced lifters
'Just do chin-ups for biceps' or 'bench for triceps' is minimalist garbage advice, usually from people with small arms
You do not need five types of cable rows; one big pull covers the bases, but do not rely only on deadlifts for lats either
Collecting and rotating many programs like Pokemon cards is why some people do not progress
Reductionism, cutting pieces out of a complex program without understanding their interactions, gives simplistic programs; perfectionism, asking how to make it better, gives simplified ones
Keeping only the squat cuts the tree of specificity from its roots; variations and accessories feed the main lift
A program should lay the tracks for your progress; minimalists who blame the lifter for lack of results are making excuses
Build a program like a canvas: start sparse and add a little at a time, three sets here or there, until you reach stability
exercises: max shoulder flexion, fixed shoulder, move only elbow
maximal long head stretch; swinging version becomes a lat pullover
elbows at sides, no shoulder lift
lifting elbows recruits shoulders, not more biceps
